opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the OCR framing undersells what's interesting about it. The headline result is that you can render text as an image, run it through a vision encoder, and get something like a ten-times compression in token count while still decoding the original text quite accurately. People read that as "a better OCR model," but to me the real question it raises is about context compression for long-context modeling.

Coming from the efficient-attention and linear-RNN side, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to keep a long history without paying quadratic cost or storing a huge KV cache. Most of the approaches we work on compress in the model's own latent space: a recurrent state, a fixed-size memory, chunked summaries. What DeepSeek showed is a different route: use the visual modality as the compression channel. A page of text becomes a small number of vision tokens, and the model can still recover most of the content. That's a kind of optical memory, and they even sketched the idea of progressively downsampling older context, like blurring older memories, which loosely mirrors human forgetting.

That said, I'd be careful about overinterpreting it. First, decoding accuracy at ten-times compression is good, but it drops quite a bit as you push to twenty-times, and reconstruction accuracy isn't the same as the model being able to *reason* over that compressed context. OCR is the easiest possible downstream task: you just need to read it back. Whether a language model can do multi-hop retrieval or in-context learning over vision-compressed history is a much harder and largely open question.

Second, there's an argument that this says less about images being magical and more about text tokenization being wasteful. Subword tokens are a pretty inefficient representation, and a vision encoder with patch-level features is effectively learning a denser, continuous encoding. So you could ask: why go through pixels at all? Could you learn a continuous text compressor directly? I think that's a legitimate research direction, and the OCR paper is a nice existence proof that such dense representations are recoverable.

So overall I find it very stimulating, maybe more as a provocation than a finished answer. It pushes the community to think about memory and compression as first-class design problems rather than just making attention windows longer, and that's very much aligned with what I care about.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the paper is interesting, but maybe not for the reason the headline suggested. People read "OCR" and assumed it was a vision paper. To me it's really a context compression paper that happens to use vision as the medium.

The core observation is pretty simple. If you render text into an image and encode it with a vision encoder, you can represent roughly ten tokens of text with one vision token and still decode it back almost perfectly. Push to twenty-to-one and you start losing information, but it degrades gracefully rather than falling off a cliff. So the question they're really asking is: what is the information density of a token, and are we wasting a lot of capacity by treating every text token as equally expensive?

From my side, working on linear attention and efficient sequence modeling, that resonates. We spend a lot of effort making the per-token cost cheaper, whether that's through recurrent state, chunked computation, or hybrid layers. DeepSeek is attacking the same problem from the other direction, reducing the number of tokens before the sequence model even sees them. Those two approaches are complementary, not competing. You can have a model with a compressed memory and also feed it a compressed input.

The part I find most speculative, and also most fun, is the forgetting analogy. They suggest you could render older context at progressively lower resolution, so recent context stays sharp and distant context blurs out. That's basically a learned decay schedule, which is exactly what gating does in linear attention. It's a bit hand-wavy right now, there's no strong experiment showing it works for long multi-turn reasoning, but the intuition is right. Not all of the past deserves the same precision.

What I'd caution against is over-reading the results. The benchmark is document OCR, which is a very structured, redundant kind of text. Compressing a dense math proof or code is a different story, and we don't yet know whether a model can reason over compressed vision tokens as well as it reasons over raw text. It's a good proof of concept with a clean idea, which is what I like about DeepSeek's papers generally. They tend to find one simple thing and show it works, rather than stacking ten tricks.
